post1.text:
Most companies stall between $50M and $500M not because of bad strategy, but because leadership never evolved past the founder's original instincts.

Adding senior executives is not a scaling strategy. It is a symptom of one. When companies like Buffini and Company bring on multiple leaders at once to accelerate growth, the real test is not who they hired. It is whether the existing leadership structure can absorb and direct that new capacity without losing coherence.

Here is what leaders at this stage consistently get wrong:

1. They hire for function and ignore for culture fit at the operating level, not just values on a poster.
2. They assume new executives will self-integrate. They will not. Onboarding at the senior level requires intentional architecture.
3. They confuse team expansion with leadership maturity. Those are two different things.

Scaling a company past $100M demands that leaders stop operating like they did at $30M. The role changes before the title does.

What is the leadership behavior in your company that made sense at $20M but is now quietly limiting your growth?

post2.text:
A recent piece in HousingWire covered Buffini and Company adding three senior executives to scale their coaching business. It is a smart move, and it reflects a pattern we see often with companies pushing past growth plateaus.

Here is what most coverage misses: the hire is never the hard part. The hard part is building the leadership infrastructure that makes those hires productive within 90 days instead of 18 months.

At Autobahn, we work with companies scaling from $50M to $500M and beyond. The firms that get executive hiring right treat it as an operating system upgrade, not just a talent acquisition. Structure, accountability, and clarity of decision rights have to come first.

If you are adding senior leadership to drive growth, ask yourself whether your operating model is ready to leverage them. Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMicEFVX3lxTE80SmJLNXdFS1VDcE9QNXQ2YzNFUDNUSzItcWljNWEyb2NEUVJ0UzdweEIzaVZyclAyWk5fcW54Nlo2U21GSVVoMHFJaVpLSFdaMU1tMXRIWU8wMTJvc3RJNTM5VkhoaVFxZnZFM0VlWVU

post3.text:
When Buffini and Company announced the addition of three senior executives to scale their business, it raised a question that Katherine Slain addresses directly in Chapter 1 of our upcoming book.

The chapter is called Lead Like Lives Depend On It, and the title is not an accident.

Katherine makes the case that leadership at scale is categorically different from leadership at startup or early growth. The stakes are higher, the blind spots are more expensive, and the margin for letting the wrong habits persist gets thinner the bigger you grow.

One insight she surfaces early: the leaders who scale companies successfully are not the ones who work harder. They are the ones who recognize which version of themselves has to change, and act on it before the business forces them to.

There is a lot more where that came from.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most business owners think about their exit too late. By the time you're ready to sell, the multiple is already set.

Here's what the most sophisticated sellers understand: your valuation is built years before you go to market, not during the deal process. Forbes recently explored how proactive exit planning, started well in advance, consistently produces better outcomes than reactive selling under pressure.

Three things leaders at the $50M+ level should be doing right now:

1. Clean up your revenue mix. Recurring, contracted revenue commands a premium. One-time project work drags your multiple down, even if total revenue looks strong.

2. Reduce key-person dependency. If your company cannot run without you for 90 days, buyers discount the price. Period.

3. Build financial reporting that speaks to acquirers. EBITDA adjustments, clean audits, and forward-looking metrics matter more than historical topline growth.

Your exit strategy is not an event. It is an operating discipline.

What is one thing you would change about your business today if you knew a buyer was evaluating it right now?

post2.text:
A recent piece from J.P. Morgan Private Bank walks through the core exit strategy options available to business owners, from strategic sales to private equity recapitalizations to family transfers.

It is a solid overview. But here is what it does not address: for companies in the $50M to $500M range, the choice of exit path is only half the equation. The other half is whether your business is actually ready to survive the scrutiny that comes with any of those options.

Buyers and investors at this level dig deep. They look at customer concentration, management bench strength, margin trends, and operational documentation. If those are not in order, the deal stalls or the price drops.

Scaling companies need to pressure-test their readiness before they ever take a meeting.

Read the full J.P. Morgan breakdown here and then ask yourself if your business would hold up under that lens: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMitwFBVV95cUxOalJUT0c3NEFPTndZX08zeGN0dXVFOEJVcmVLRml0QUNjb2xXU3Nxd2ZjOW1mUVUtc0F6SDZ0M056b2Rpd21ZZWF6aVBpOHZESjRiMEtKYk13Sm52VTJJTzV5ZzhFVTE5LVVtcVN4aVpiUzJYUUEtclFONlM4S0NzS3owaFRDT3p6Z2NoZlhjSUh1QnhsWTkyT3pKQkJZR3YxWnZHSHpHTDQ3MEtSRDdBb1JDTVJrb1U

post3.text:
Exit planning conversations are everywhere right now. Forbes, Silicon Valley Bank, J.P. Morgan are all publishing guidance on when to sell and how to think about it.

But most of that advice skips the hardest part: maximizing your multiple before you ever sit across the table from a buyer.

Chapter 2 of Rock Your Business, titled Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit, tackles exactly that. Written by Paul Belair and George Hohman, the chapter lays out what actually moves the needle on valuation for companies in the $50M to $500M range. One thing they make clear early: the factors that increase your multiple are not the same factors that grew your revenue. That distinction changes everything about how you should be running your business today.

post1.text:
Most strategic plans fail not because the strategy was wrong, but because execution was an afterthought.

Companies that have crossed the $50M mark often have strong instincts and hard-won experience. What they frequently lack is a structured system that connects big-picture direction to daily decisions. When Indra Group recently restructured its entire management committee to align with a new operating model, it was a public acknowledgment of something most leaders resist admitting: your org structure either enables your strategy or quietly kills it.

Here is what scaling companies get wrong most often:

1. Strategy is created at the top and handed down, rather than built with the people responsible for executing it.
2. Annual planning cycles move too slowly for companies growing at this pace. Quarterly rhythm matters more.
3. Accountability is assumed, not designed. Without clear ownership at every level, priorities collapse under pressure.

You can have the right destination in mind and still end up nowhere if the vehicle is not built for the road.

What is the single biggest gap between your strategy and your execution right now?

post2.text:
A recent announcement from Indra Group caught our attention: the company reorganized its entire management committee to bring it in line with a new operating model.

For most observers, this is a footnote. For leaders scaling past $50M, it should be a signal.

Structure follows strategy. Or it should. The problem we see constantly with growing companies is that leadership teams hold onto org structures built for an earlier, smaller version of the business. The result is friction, slow decisions, and a strategy that never quite lands.

If your management team is still set up the way it was three years ago, it may be quietly working against your next three years.

This is one of the most underestimated levers in scaling. Is your structure built for where you are going, or just where you have been?

Read the full Indra Group announcement here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMivAFBVV95cUxNeXp3anE4OVZMTDNtYnlEcjRoTHhRVDUzQnIyckplanJXWk5yelNWaklIeEtZOVVmUVdoZ19raGk5dkdNRVBic2FLcFo4OE4yc3ptc2wtUGFlYVA4NVE4bl9aT0JLZnVma0hMZFl6aGlkSjVUMUlQcUlEczB3Q25LVzlMWGk3azNqbU43cWRTREdsMl9lNnZiYnRhSEZUWHh2ZFZONGVkXzczNlA5NjZ3eklwXzRWeDc1RGJwVA

post3.text:
What can selling fish food and Nike shoes teach you about strategic planning at scale? More than most MBA programs.

In Chapter 3 of our upcoming book Rock Your Business, titled 'What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes,' authors Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall draw on real experience across wildly different industries to show why execution frameworks that work at $10M often become the very thing that stalls growth at $100M.

One of the sharpest insights in this chapter: the plans that scale are not the most complex ones. They are the ones that every person in the company can actually understand and act on.

When Indra Group reorganized its leadership to match its strategy, they were doing exactly what Rafa and Jim describe. Alignment is not a soft concept. It is a growth driver.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M think they have a sales strategy. They don't. They have a collection of habits that worked when the company was smaller.

Here's the uncomfortable truth: a sales strategy that got you to $50M will actively work against you on the way to $500M.

Recent research from Forrester confirms what we see inside scaling companies every day. B2B buying decisions no longer sit with one person. Multiple stakeholders across multiple functions are involved in every major purchase. If your sales motion still targets a single contact, you are leaving revenue on the table by design.

Three things leaders at this growth stage need to face:

1. Your sales process was built for a buyer that no longer exists.
2. Revenue is now a cross-functional outcome, not a sales department metric.
3. Without a real strategy, every quarter is a donation to your competitors.

So ask yourself this: if your top salesperson left tomorrow, would your revenue system still function?

post2.text:
A recent piece in McKinsey and Company lays out something scaling companies cannot afford to ignore. The economics of B2B growth have shifted. The threshold you need to hit just to survive has moved, and the gap between companies that thrive and those that stall is widening faster than most leaders realize.

At Autobahn, we see this play out with companies in the $50M to $500M range all the time. Growth stops feeling inevitable and starts feeling fragile. The difference almost always comes down to whether the company has a real sales strategy or is just running on momentum from earlier years.

Momentum is not a plan. If your growth engine is not deliberately designed, it is already losing efficiency.

Read the McKinsey piece and then ask your leadership team: what is our actual strategy for the next stage of growth?

post3.text:
Forrester's latest research makes one thing clear: winning in B2B today requires every function in the company working together around a shared revenue strategy. Sales alone cannot carry it.

Chapter 4 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, tackles this head on. The chapter is titled Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation, and it was written by Deb and Brandon, who have worked inside enough scaling companies to know exactly where the cracks form.

One thing they address that most leaders overlook: the difference between having a sales team and having a sales system. Those are not the same thing, and confusing them is expensive.

If you are running a company between $50M and $500M, this chapter will challenge how you think about revenue at a structural level.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling people get when they interact with your company, and most $50M+ leaders are completely blind to what that feeling actually is.

Adweek recently covered how Campari manages a portfolio of iconic brands by anchoring every decision to culture and sensory identity. That is a lesson most mid-market companies skip entirely.

Here is what scaling companies get wrong about branding:

1. They confuse visibility with identity. Spending more on ads does not fix a brand that feels inconsistent at every touchpoint.

2. They brand for founders, not buyers. Your story matters, but your customer's transformation matters more.

3. They treat brand as a one-time project. At $50M and beyond, brand is an operating system, not a campaign.

Ulta's CMO put it plainly: brand building and performance marketing are not separate functions. They feed each other. If your team treats them as separate budgets with separate goals, you are leaving growth on the table.

What does your brand actually feel like to a first-time customer who has never heard your name before?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive on Ulta's CMO caught our attention, and it should catch yours too.

The core idea: brand building and omnichannel marketing are not competing priorities. They are the same priority. Ulta has built one of the most loyal retail customer bases in the country by refusing to treat brand as separate from the buying experience.

For companies scaling past $50M, this is a real gap. Leadership tends to chase performance metrics while brand coherence quietly erodes. By the time the numbers show it, the damage is done.

The fix is not a rebrand. It is a deliberate decision to treat every customer touchpoint as a brand moment, not just a transaction.

Read the full piece here and ask yourself where your brand experience breaks down: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPRlFnSEozTXJJdnl5aWFJQTFGR0tkcnhrUnUyOTNZNlIwcHZiLWFnbm0tQ0FWZEZCTWZvdUFQeEFvQkIwOHdpMmZBR3I5WmNjRmFYb0xJMGhQWmJHYUdWUVdyWndOWTYwR1ZQQ2E4V1dMV2NrT0hpRzNaU1VKdUdoZHMwSFB4SlhYTkZKZ2hDdEdsSkJ6TW91UTZTWlNGaGVmcUE

post3.text:
Campari does not just sell drinks. It sells a feeling, a ritual, a sense of belonging to something storied and alive. That kind of brand intentionality does not happen by accident.

In Chapter 5 of Rock Your Business, titled "What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?", authors Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West challenge leaders to think about brand the way a customer actually experiences it: sensorially, emotionally, and consistently across every interaction.

Most companies at the $50M mark have grown fast enough that their brand has drifted. What got them here was hustle. What gets them to $500M is coherence.

Kayli and Yasmin lay out a framework for diagnosing exactly where your brand experience breaks down and how to fix it before growth exposes the cracks.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost problem disguised as ambition.

SHRM's latest research on 2026 hiring trends makes this clear: the companies pulling ahead are not the ones posting the most roles. They are the ones obsessing over precision, hiring fewer people who fit more specifically, and building systems that retain them longer.

For leaders scaling past $50M, that reframe changes everything.

Three things worth considering:

1. Your next hire should solve a defined constraint, not fill a vague capacity gap. If you cannot name the exact bottleneck, you are not ready to hire.

2. Retention is a talent acquisition strategy. Every departure resets momentum and burns recruiting budget you could deploy elsewhere.

3. Culture fit is not a personality test. It is whether someone can execute inside your specific operating model at your current stage of growth.

Scaling companies that treat talent as a precision instrument outperform those that treat it as a volume game.

What would change in your next hire if you asked "does this solve our most expensive problem" before posting the role?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SHRM titled "Precision Over Scale: The New Rules of Hiring in 2026" puts a number on something we see inside scaling companies every week: the cost of hiring broadly instead of hiring right.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this is not an HR conversation. It is an operations conversation. Undisciplined hiring at this stage bloats overhead, slows decision-making, and introduces cultural drift at exactly the moment you need alignment most.

The leaders who scale well are not adding headcount to solve revenue problems. They are building talent engines with defined intake criteria, clear performance expectations, and accountability structures that hold from day one.

If your talent strategy still looks like it did when you were a $20M company, it is worth a hard look.

Read the full SHRM piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMioAFBVV95cUxPRFVYR0VscXJpMmVqV2dwazJDTkstVDJTNG9uTlZlWHJPVkFqQ0MzZTRQSUYwUDZweWw2dE52THZKSnhBTzQtb1g5UUYzbmJTbjFJcXlVYno2ZzU4aE0yNVRwN2RIN05xTWJVWnZQejVyY2xRNmJ2SF83QmVHel9GYmdWTEdEMWZLMVk5OThMNTF0TmdKR1F4bG84cnZRZ0FU?oc=5

SHRM's reporting on precision hiring in 2026 is validating something our contributors have been saying for years.

In Chapter 6 of Rock Your Business, "The Talent Engine," co-author Caleb Hawkins makes a point that stops a lot of leaders cold: most scaling companies do not have a talent shortage. They have a talent architecture problem.

The chapter lays out how companies in the $50M to $500M range need to stop treating hiring as a reactive function and start building it as a repeatable system with its own inputs, outputs, and performance metrics.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better decisions. They make slower ones.

Most leadership teams at $50M+ companies are not suffering from a lack of data. They are drowning in it. Hootsuite recently published a list of 31 social media metrics worth tracking. Thirty-one. For one channel. That number is not a toolkit. It is a trap.

Here is what we see consistently with scaling companies:

First, when every metric is a priority, none of them are. Leaders spend meeting time debating dashboards instead of making calls.

Second, the KPIs being tracked are often measuring activity, not outcomes. Busy metrics protect underperformance.

Third, the companies growing fastest tend to have fewer metrics on the leadership scorecard, not more. Clarity at the top cascades down. Noise does too.

The discipline is not in adding another metric. It is in having the conviction to cut the ones that are not driving decisions.

How many KPIs on your current scorecard have actually changed a leadership decision in the last 90 days?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Business.com walked through 14 tools companies can use to track KPIs. Solid overview, and the tools are legitimate.

But here is what the article does not address: the tool is rarely the problem.

For companies scaling past $50M, the failure point is almost never the software. It is the lack of agreement on which numbers actually matter and who owns them. We have seen leadership teams with beautiful, expensive dashboards that nobody looks at between quarterly reviews.

Tracking tools create visibility. They do not create accountability. That requires a different conversation at the leadership level.

If your team is evaluating KPI software right now, spend equal time defining the 5 to 7 metrics that would genuinely change your decisions if they moved. Build from there.

Full article worth reading: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMingFBVV95cUxQcWNPSTVTUDVYYURoVkZKa0ItNEtQbmJqWlNJTlIzUVZqclAxMHFaajNobC1JbGNkZGZVajN6MWJLT1pJcXktVG10VG8zUUljdU43NU5WR1cyNDB4QkxONlJkb3hJR2FfNzdGZHd1VWhPbTktdU1vdTEzamFWY2ZFVDNKUFIwRG91ZDdWU1UyN2twNFpLd1JjU3EzTUpjdw?oc=5

post3.text:
There is a chapter in our upcoming book that we think a lot of leadership teams need to read before their next planning cycle.

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business is titled "Death by KPIs." Co-authored by Héctor Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, it confronts something most consultants will not say out loud: the metrics systems inside scaling companies often create the illusion of performance management while actively blocking real accountability.

One idea the chapter surfaces is that the problem is rarely too few KPIs. It is that the wrong people own the wrong numbers, and nobody has ever formally decided what a good result actually looks like.

If your leadership team is spending more time building reports than acting on them, this chapter will feel uncomfortably familiar.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
AI is making your team more productive. That is exactly why your revenue isn't growing.

Most leaders treat AI as an efficiency play. Faster outputs, leaner headcount, lower costs. But according to recent research, companies across industries are watching productivity climb while revenue growth stays flat. The gains aren't compounding. They're evaporating.

Here's what scaling companies need to understand:

1. Productivity without redeployment is just savings. If your team does the same work faster and you don't redirect that capacity toward growth, you've optimized a treadmill.

2. AI adoption without a strategic use case is a science project. Knowing what problem you're solving before you deploy the tool is what separates leaders from experimenters.

3. The companies winning right now are using AI to make better decisions faster, not just to cut time from existing tasks. That's a fundamentally different implementation mindset.

You don't need more AI tools. You need a clearer answer to one question: what will you do with the hours you get back?

What's your answer?

post2.text:
A recent piece in the Cyprus Mail landed on something most leadership teams aren't talking about openly: AI is lifting productivity across the board, but companies are struggling to translate those gains into actual revenue growth.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly with companies in the $50M to $500M range. Leaders invest in the technology, see real efficiency wins, and then wonder why the top line isn't moving. The problem isn't the tool. It's the absence of a deliberate plan for what happens after the efficiency kicks in.

If your AI implementation doesn't have a defined growth outcome attached to it, you're not behind on technology. You're behind on strategy.

That's the conversation worth having. Read the full article and then ask yourself where your productivity gains are actually going.

post1.text:
Imposter syndrome is not a weakness. It is a signal that you are operating at the edge of your capability, which is exactly where growth happens.

Forbes Australia recently explored why high achievers tend to carry self-doubt all the way to the top. The finding should reframe how leaders at scaling companies think about this entirely.

Here is what matters if you are running a $50M+ business:

1. The leaders who feel most like frauds are often the ones making the boldest moves. Comfort and imposter syndrome do not coexist.

2. Suppressing it costs you. Leaders who hide self-doubt from their teams create cultures where no one admits uncertainty, and bad decisions live longer than they should.

3. The goal is not to eliminate it. The goal is to stop letting it make decisions for you.

Your team is watching how you handle doubt more closely than they are watching your wins.

So here is the real question: If your best leaders all feel like imposters sometimes, what does that tell you about the standard you have actually built?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Campaign US made an argument worth sitting with: stop trying to outgrow imposter syndrome and start putting it to work.

For companies scaling past $50M, this reframe is not just interesting, it is operationally important. At that stage, your leadership team is making decisions in territory they have never navigated before. Self-doubt is going to show up. The question is whether it sharpens their thinking or shuts them down.

At Autobahn, we work with leaders who have built remarkable companies and still wonder if they belong in the room. The ones who scale successfully are not the ones who feel the most confident. They are the ones who have learned to act clearly in spite of the discomfort.

Read the full piece and think about where this dynamic is already playing out on your team.

post3.text:
Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business is titled "How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?" and it tackles something most business books refuse to touch directly: what happens to a leader's psychology when the company outgrows who they used to be.

Authored by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo, this chapter does not offer a pep talk. It gives scaling leaders a clear-eyed way to understand why imposter syndrome intensifies as success grows, not in spite of it.

One thing the chapter makes clear early: the feeling of not belonging in your own company is not random. It follows a pattern. And once you see the pattern, you can stop being managed by it.

This is the kind of insight that changes how you show up in the room that matters most.

post1.text:
The founders who burn out at $200M didn't fail at strategy. They failed at designing their own life.

Most leaders scaling past $50M treat personal planning as a reward for later. Something they'll figure out once the company hits the next milestone. That moment never comes, and the cost is steep.

Morgan Stanley recently highlighted what happens to entrepreneurs after a liquidity event: many report a profound loss of identity and purpose. Not because they lacked wealth, but because they never built a life outside the business to return to.

Three things high-growth leaders consistently underinvest in:

1. Deciding in advance what success actually looks like for them personally, not just the company
2. Building relationships and routines that exist completely outside work hours
3. Creating a personal vision with the same rigor they apply to a business plan

Your company can scale. Your calendar, your health, and your relationships cannot be backfilled later.

What would you protect first if your company tripled in size next year?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune, produced in partnership with Morgan Stanley, maps out what life looks like for entrepreneurs after selling their business. It is a thoughtful roadmap covering identity, finances, and purpose.

Here is what most scaling companies miss: that conversation needs to start long before an exit.

At Autobahn, we work with leaders navigating the $50M to $500M stretch. The ones who struggle most after a major transition are those who never separated who they are from what they built. That distinction is not a soft skill. It is a business risk.

If you lead a growing company, read this piece and ask yourself whether your personal plan is keeping pace with your growth plan.

A recent Fortune article on life after selling a business asks entrepreneurs to think carefully about identity, purpose, and what comes next. It is a question most leaders defer until it is urgent.

Chapter 10 of Rock Your Business, titled Coming Up for Air, addresses exactly this. Authored by Samantha Frost and Jonathan and Katherine Slain, the chapter goes further than work-life balance advice. It challenges leaders scaling past $50M to design a life plan with the same intentionality they bring to their growth strategy.

One thing the chapter makes clear: the structure that helps you build a company can quietly become the thing that costs you everything else. Knowing how to separate the two is a skill, and it can be developed.
